subtopics.title: The US-Saudi 123 Agreement
subtopics.summary: The US and Saudi Arabia signed a Section 123 Civil Nuclear Cooperation Agreement with a bilateral safeguards arrangement, for 30 years. Section 123 of the US Atomic Energy Act, 1954 makes such agreements a legally binding prerequisite for significant US nuclear cooperation. The deal is reportedly linked to Riyadh joining the Abraham Accords and normalising relations with Israel.
facts: Signed for 30 years by US Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman.
Named after Section 123 of the US Atomic Energy Act, 1954.
A 123 Agreement is a legally binding prerequisite for significant US nuclear cooperation with another country.
Cooperation may cover reactors, nuclear materials, components, equipment, technology and technical expertise.
Bilateral Safeguards Arrangement ensures civilian nuclear materials are not diverted towards weapons.
Saudi Arabia may undertake uranium enrichment in facilities developed with US support, subject to safeguards.
The agreement does not require Saudi Arabia to adopt the IAEA Additional Protocol.
The agreement is subject to a review period of 90 legislative days by the US Congress.
The deal is reportedly linked to Riyadh joining the Abraham Accords and normalising relations with Israel.

subtopics.title: Saudi Arabia's Nuclear Vision
subtopics.summary: Saudi Arabia's nuclear programme is built on four drivers: energy diversification, large-scale desalination, meeting cooling demand and strategic technology development. The Kingdom signed the NPT in 1988 and launched its National Atomic Energy Project in 2017. The new deal drops the earlier Israel normalisation condition and allows flexibility on domestic enrichment.
facts: Nuclear power lets Saudi Arabia reduce its heavy dependence on crude oil and natural gas for electricity.
The nuclear programme provides the massive energy input needed for large-scale water desalination.
Nuclear-generated electricity provides a steady supply for air-conditioning and cooling systems.
A nuclear programme grants access to advanced technology and reinforces Saudi status as a regional energy power.
Saudi Arabia signed the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty in 1988.
Saudi Arabia launched its National Atomic Energy Project in 2017.
The earlier Gold Standard required no domestic uranium enrichment or reprocessing, and normalised ties with Israel.
The new deal drops the Israel normalisation condition and allows flexibility for US-supported domestic enrichment.

subtopics.title: Nuclear Weapons History and Treaties
subtopics.summary: Nuclear weapons were developed in the US-led Manhattan Project, with the Trinity test in July 1945 and bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945. Treaties then tried to limit testing and spread, including the PTBT (1963), NPT (1968), CTBT (1996) and TPNW (2017). The IAEA (1957) and the NSG (1974-75) were created to manage peaceful use and export controls.
facts: The Manhattan Project was a secret US-led programme with the UK and Canada; Gen. Leslie Groves led engineering and J. Robert Oppenheimer led science.
The Trinity Test in July 1945 was the first-ever nuclear explosion, conducted in the New Mexico desert.
Little Boy (uranium gun-type) was dropped on Hiroshima on 6 August 1945; Fat Man (plutonium implosion-type) was dropped on Nagasaki on 9 August 1945.
The Partial Test Ban Treaty (1963) banned tests in the atmosphere, outer space and underwater, but not underground.
The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (1968) was signed to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons.
The IAEA, established in 1957, promotes peaceful uses of atomic energy and oversees safeguards.
The Nuclear Suppliers Group (1974-75) was formed to control the export of nuclear materials and technology.
The CTBT (1996) was adopted by the UN to ban all nuclear explosions and has not yet entered into force.
The TPNW (2017) entered into force in 2021 and is the first legally binding treaty to comprehensively ban nuclear weapons; nuclear powers have not joined.
North Korea withdrew from the NPT in 2003 and later conducted nuclear tests.

subtopics.title: India's Atomic Energy Journey
subtopics.summary: India's programme was organised through the Atomic Energy Commission (1948) and the Department of Atomic Energy (1954), with Dr Homi J. Bhabha leading the AEC. Key milestones include the 1974 Pokhran-I test and the 1998 Pokhran-II tests. The 2008 Indo-US 123 Agreement ended India's nuclear isolation and was a landmark precedent.
facts: The Atomic Energy Commission was set up in 1948, with Dr Homi J. Bhabha as its chairman.
The Department of Atomic Energy was created in 1954 under the Prime Minister's Office.
The Atomic Energy Act, 1962 is India's primary law for nuclear energy.
Tarapur Atomic Power Station, India's first commercial nuclear plant, was commissioned in 1969 under Atoms for Peace.
Pokhran-I (1974), the Smiling Buddha test, was India's first peaceful nuclear explosion.
Dhruva, India's largest research reactor, was commissioned at BARC in 1985.
Pokhran-II (Operation Shakti) in 1998 led to India being declared a nuclear-weapon state.
India's Nuclear Doctrine, adopted in 2003, follows No First Use and Credible Minimum Deterrence.
The Indo-US Civil Nuclear Agreement (123 Agreement), signed in 2008, ended India's nuclear isolation.
India is a Non-NPT nuclear weapons state, which makes the 2008 agreement a landmark precedent.

quizzes.passage: Saudi Arabia's nuclear vision is built on a set of four drivers that shape the direction of its programme. The Kingdom signed the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty in 1988, and it launched its National Atomic Energy Project in 2017. Nuclear power is part of a wider plan for energy and industry, and each driver addresses a different practical need. The programme is also tied to the Kingdom's standing in the Middle East. The new civil nuclear arrangement with the United States forms the latest stage of this effort. It sets the terms for cooperation on reactors, materials, components and technical expertise. Such cooperation falls under a legally binding framework that is linked to a specific section of American law. Within this structure, the agreement includes a bilateral safeguards arrangement, which is meant to ensure that civilian nuclear materials are not diverted to weapons. The agreement is also subject to a review period by the US Congress. Taken together, these elements show how the Kingdom's ambitions link energy planning with international commitments and regional influence. The arrangement is designed to support long-term cooperation in the civil nuclear field, and its structure reflects the importance of verification. Such a structure allows the parties to keep civilian activities within agreed limits.

quizzes.passage: Saudi Arabia has set out a nuclear programme that rests on four drivers, and the Kingdom's ambitions reach well beyond electricity alone. The country signed the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty in 1988 and launched its National Atomic Energy Project in 2017. The programme is linked to economic and industrial growth, and it is connected to the Kingdom's place in the Middle East. The United States and Saudi Arabia have now signed a civil nuclear cooperation agreement, which forms the latest stage in this relationship. Such an agreement falls under a legal framework that is treated as a prerequisite for significant nuclear cooperation with other countries. The framework covers the transfer of reactors, components and technical expertise. Any nuclear activity carried out under it remains subject to verification, and the two parties have agreed on arrangements for this purpose. The agreement also reflects changes to earlier conditions that the United States had placed on cooperation with the Kingdom. The agreement is subject to a review period by the United States Congress. Each of the four drivers serves a different purpose, so the programme cannot be understood through any single goal alone. These developments show how Saudi Arabia's nuclear plans are linked to its energy goals, its industrial aims and its diplomatic relations.

quizzes.passage: India's atomic energy programme grew through a set of institutions, each created for a particular purpose. The Atomic Energy Commission was one of the early bodies, and it was later joined by a separate department that brought the programme's administration under one roof. Scientific work was carried out at several research centres, supported by reactors built for that purpose. Power generation followed when a commercial plant was set up under the Atoms for Peace effort. The country also carried out nuclear tests in the 1970s and again in the late 1990s, and these tests changed India's standing in the world. Its nuclear doctrine, adopted in 2003, set out the principles that would guide the use of its arsenal. Legal foundations for nuclear energy were also put in place through a statute passed in the twentieth century. Research reactors, power plants and legal instruments each contributed to this progress. In 2008, an agreement with the United States allowed civilian nuclear trade with India, which had been excluded from such trade for a long period. The sequence of these developments, from the early institutions to the 2008 agreement, spans several decades. The agreement remains an important reference point in discussions about how India fits into the global nuclear order.

quizzes.passage: India's nuclear effort was organised through a series of institutions, each set up for a distinct task. The Atomic Energy Commission was one of these bodies, and it was later complemented by a department that gave the programme a formal administrative base. Research was carried out at several centres, and the country built reactors to support scientific work. Power generation began with a commercial plant, which was built as part of the Atoms for Peace effort. Over the following decades, India carried out a series of tests that transformed its position in the world. Its doctrine for the use of its arsenal was adopted in 2003 and set out principles for how that arsenal would be used. The legal basis for India's atomic work was also set out in a statute enacted in the twentieth century. In 2008, an agreement with the United States opened the way for civil nuclear trade with India, a step that reversed years of exclusion from such commerce. Together, these milestones show how the programme developed from its early institutions into a set of policies that shape India's place in global nuclear affairs. Research reactors, power plants and legal instruments each contributed to this progress, and the sequence of events spans several decades.
